newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish MPs vote to investigate state-mafia links.
newsitem.headline: Turkish MPs vote to investigate state-mafia links.

text.p: Turkey's parliament on Tuesday voted to investigate alleged ties between the powerful state security apparatus and organised crime following a car crash linking a top police official and a gangster.

"When I was walking in the market the other day, people kept asking me: What is going to happen with the politics-mafia- police thing? Well we are about to vote to form a commission to clear up all this," Suha Tanik, an opposition MP who proposed the investigation, told parliament just before the vote.
Parliament voted unanimously for a full-scale parliamentary inquiry. The findings of the inquiry have no legal consequences.

Former Interior Minister Mehmet Agar resigned from his post on Friday in the wake of the crash, in which a mobster wanted for political killings and drug dealing died in the same car as a senior security official and a former beauty queen.
A Kurdish warlord, who serves as a government deputy in parliament, was injured in the crash. Associates say he is suffering from "amnesia".

"If there had not been that crash, maybe we would not be discussing this subject in the parliament assembly today, despite several similar motions already pending," said Justice Minister Sevket Kazan.

"As the government, we think it positive that this affair is being discussed in parliament and that MPs...are going to be making statements," he said. "We are focusing on this incident and will continue to do so until things are cleared up."
Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, and Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller, who also holds the deputy premiership, did not attend the session. Ciller returned late on Tuesday from a one-day visit to Jordan.

At the start of the parliamentary session, speaker Yasin Hatipoglu announced that President Suleyman Demirel had approved the appointment of Meral Aksener as Agar's successor. She is Turkey's first woman interior minister.
"She has taken over the post at a really critical time," Hatipoglu said. "She has taken on a very difficult task at a time when there are many unpleasant smells around."
When she took over from Agar on Monday, Aksener vowed to fight against organised crime and the ministry said in a statement that it was considering instituting its own inquiry into the affair.
The chief prosecutor at Istanbul state security court on Tuesday opened an investigation into the crash.
But political analysts were sceptical that the debate and the flurry of inquiries would amount to anything more than the usual lip service paid to the subject from time to time.

"We do not expect anything to come out of this debate because all those who are represented in parliament today have been in charge of running the country at one point or other in the past decade and thus have a share in the mess," wrote Ilnur Cevik in the English-language Turkish Daily News.
"There are too many people in high places who are in this right up to their necks," Cevik wrote in his editorial.
Opposition MPs expressed the same fears:
"I hope there will be some results this time," said Ugur Aksoz, of the main opposition Motherland Party, listing a catalogue of past allegations still unresolved.
Erbakan and Ciller have both denied any link between the crash and Agar's resignation. But Agar said he resigned to clear the way for a parliamentary investigation.
Media reports say Agar stayed in the same hotel as the crash victims in the Aegean resort of Kusadasi before the accident.
